content: Providencia is a genus of Gram-negative, motile bacteria belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae. Certain strains, such as Providencia stuartii, are opportunistic pathogens in humans and are known to cause urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly in individuals with long-term indwelling urinary catheters or those with extensive and severe burns. Other strains, such as Providencia burhodogranariea and Providencia sneebia, have been identified in the hemolymph of Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies. Some strains of Providencia are sensitive to ampicillin. Providencia stuartii Providencia stuartii is the most frequently encountered species of Providencia that causes human infections. It is an opportunistic pathogen, particularly affecting patients with severe burns or those with long-term indwelling urinary catheters. Elderly individuals are at a higher risk of developing infections caused by P. stuartii. In animals, P. stuartii can lead to neonatal diarrhea in dairy cows. In humans, this bacterium is most commonly isolated from urine but can also be found in stool, blood, sputum, skin, and wound cultures. Bloodstream infections caused by P. stuartii are typically of urinary origin and are associated with a condition known as purple urine bag syndrome. Clinical manifestations of P. stuartii septicemia include fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. Providencia rettgeri Providencia rettgeri is another Gram-negative bacterium that is commonly found in both aquatic and terrestrial environments. It can be cultured at 37°C using nutrient agar or nutrient broth. This species was first identified in 1904 during an epidemic in waterfowl. Strains of P. rettgeri have also been isolated from nematodes. In humans, P. rettgeri is an opportunistic pathogen that resides in the gastrointestinal tract and is a significant cause of traveler’s diarrhea. It has also been implicated in urinary tract infections and eye infections. Diagnostic Characteristics of Providencia rettgeri Providencia rettgeri can be identified based on its motility and its ability to produce acid from mannitol. It does not produce gas from glucose, does not ferment lactose, and does not produce hydrogen sulfide or acid from xylose. Antimicrobial Treatment for Providencia Infections For complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), bacteremia, or acute prostatitis caused by Providencia species, the following antimicrobial regimens are recommended: 1. Ciprofloxacin: 500–750 mg orally every 12 hours or 400 mg intravenously every 8–12 hours. 2. Levofloxacin: 500 mg intravenously or orally every 24 hours. 3. Piperacillin-Tazobactam: 3.375 g intravenously every 6 hours. 4. Ceftriaxone: 1–2 g intravenously every 24 hours (avoid use if extended-spectrum beta-lactamase [ESBL] production is suspected or in critically ill patients). 5. Meropenem: 1 g intravenously every 8 hours (consider for critically ill patients or if ESBL production is suspected). 6. Amikacin: 7.5 mg/kg intravenously every 12 hours. 7. Gentamicin: Dosage based on susceptibility. 8. Tobramycin: Acceptable if the strain is susceptible, but many Providencia species exhibit resistance. Notes on Treatment Duration For UTIs, the typical duration of treatment is 7 days, or 3–5 days after the resolution of fever or the removal of complicating factors (e.g., catheter removal). For bacteremia, treatment duration is 10–14 days, or 3–5 days after the resolution of fever or the elimination of complicating factors. For acute prostatitis, treatment is typically 2 weeks, whereas chronic prostatitis requires 4–6 weeks of therapy. Alternative Regimen An alternative treatment option includes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) double strength (DS) orally every 12 hours for 10–14 days, or trimethoprim (TMP) 5–10 mg/kg/day intravenously every 6 hours.
